1:1.text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.

provenance.other: 'How great things the Lord' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 5:19. Luke 8:39 tells the same episode and reads 'how great things God hath done unto thee', which is not the wording here.
provenance.significance: The phrase re-enters in a different hand. At 1 Nephi 7:11 it is Nephi's rebuke to his brothers — 'how great things the Lord hath done for us' — and here it is the narrator's summary of what his father said to those same brothers. Mark's sentence is a commission: the man Jesus has just cleansed asks to follow him, is refused, and is sent home to tell his own people instead. Both Book of Mormon uses put it in the mouth of someone sent back to a hostile household to say what God has done, which is the one thing the source's context supplies and the phrase alone does not.

1:1.note: 'Lehi also spake many things unto them: how great things the Lord had done for them, in bringing them out of the land of Jerusalem.' The KJV has this formula once. The argument for it was made at 1 Nephi 7:11, where the run is eight words and the 1830 preserves 'how' against 1920's 'what' in the parallel at that verse; it is given again here because a new book is a new voice and a reader of 2 Nephi shown nothing at 1:1 has been told there is no borrowing here (ADJUDICATING §4). Note that the exposition Lehi is about to give — a deliverance recited as the warrant for present obedience — is the shape Mark 5:19 commissions.

1:7.text: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.

provenance.other: 'Iniquity shall abound' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 24:12. The KJV's other 'abound' collocations are Pauline and positive — grace, hope, love, thanksgiving.
provenance.significance: The clause Lehi uses to state the condition on which the land is cursed is the clause the Olivet discourse uses to state the condition of the last days. In Matthew it is the third of the signs — false prophets, then iniquity abounding, then love waxing cold, then the end — so the words arrive already carrying a chronology of decline, which is exactly what verses 10-12 of this chapter then supply: the people receive the blessings, reject the Holy One, and are scattered as one generation passes to another. Lehi's conditional promise is worded out of an apocalypse.

1:7.note: 'If iniquity shall abound, cursed shall be the land for their sakes.' A KJV singleton, three words long and unmistakable, and it is doing the same work in both places: naming the point at which a promised condition tips into judgment. Well below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion, but the absolute rarity is what makes it worth having.

1:7.text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

provenance.other: 'Cursed is the ground for thy sake' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:17; the only other curse-the-ground clause is Genesis 8:21's 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake'. 'For thy sake' by itself occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and cannot carry the link alone.
provenance.alternative: The Deuteronomic blessing-and-curse formularies (Deuteronomy 28:15-18) are the obvious background for a conditional land curse and share the vocabulary of cursing without the ground.
provenance.significance: Lehi has just called this a land of liberty and a land consecrated, and the sentence that states its liability is Eden's. Genesis 3:17 curses the ground because of what a man did, not because of what the ground is, and it is the KJV's founding statement that a place can be spoiled by the conduct of the people in it. That is the doctrine this chapter needs — the land is choice above all other lands and can nevertheless be cursed — and the Book of Mormon has taken it in the words of the sentence that first said it.

1:7.note: 'Cursed shall be the land for their sakes; but unto the righteous, it shall be blessed forever.' Against Genesis 3:17's 'cursed is the ground for thy sake', with 'ground' becoming 'land' and the singular becoming plural. What tells is the addition Lehi makes: Genesis has no answering blessing, and the Book of Mormon supplies one, which converts a sentence of expulsion into a conditional tenure. Proposed at moderate because the two content words that survive are 'cursed' and the 'for … sake' construction.

1:9.text: And they shall no more be a prey to the heathen, neither shall the beast of the land devour them; but they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid.

provenance.other: 'Dwell safely' occurs in nine KJV verses and 'none shall make them afraid' in four; Ezekiel 34:28 is the one verse that holds both, together with the promise that they shall 'no more be a prey to the heathen'. 'Molest' occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Leviticus 26:5-6 gives the same two promises across two verses, and the whole cluster is standard covenant-blessing language that no single verse owns.
provenance.significance: Every element of the Book of Mormon's promise is in Ezekiel 34:28 and in the same order: safety from the nations, the absence of anyone to trouble them, and dwelling safely. The one substitution is the one that matters — Ezekiel's 'none shall make them afraid' becomes 'none to molest them', a word the KJV does not use at all. The borrowing has been paraphrased at exactly the point where the source is most formulaic, which is what a writer working from memory of the sense rather than the page produces.

1:9.note: 'They shall be kept from all other nations … there shall be none to molest them, nor to take away the land of their inheritance; and they shall dwell safely forever.' Proposed on the cluster rather than on any one phrase: only Ezekiel 34:28 assembles all three promises in a single verse. Recorded at moderate because 'dwell safely' is common and the distinctive word in the Book of Mormon's clause, 'molest', is not KJV English at all.
1:9.whyNot: Nothing here is a KJV singleton, and the sheep-shepherd frame that governs Ezekiel 34 is entirely absent from Lehi's blessing. A reader could take the whole verse as generic covenant idiom and would not be obviously wrong.

1:10.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: 'Great and marvellous' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and only 15:3 attaches it to works: 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty.' The 1830 spells it 'marvellous', which is the KJV's spelling; 1920 modernized to 'marvelous' and in doing so erased the orthographic evidence of the borrowing (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: This is the fourth time in the corpus that Revelation 15:3 stands behind a Book of Mormon sentence, and Lehi takes the half of it that Nephi did not. 1 Nephi 1:14 borrowed the vocative — 'Great and marvellous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty' — from a verse Revelation itself labels 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Here the same verse supplies the works, and nine verses later, at 1:19, Lehi finishes it: 'his ways are righteousness forever' answers Revelation 15:3's 'just and true are thy ways.' A dying man's last blessing runs on the song the redeemed sing in Revelation, and Revelation names that song after the man whose deathbed charge (Deuteronomy 33) this chapter is imitating.

1:10.note: 'All men knowing the great and marvellous works of the Lord from the creation of the world.' Two KJV verses have 'great and marvellous' and both are Revelation 15; only 15:3 has it of God's works, which is the form here. The link is not a fresh discovery of the verse — 1 Nephi 1:14 established it — but the distribution within this chapter is new: 1:10 takes the works and 1:19 takes the ways, which are the two halves of the same sentence in the source, split across nine verses of a single speech. Note also 'from the creation of the world', which is itself a KJV singleton at Romans 1:20 and is filed in the register.

1:12.text: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.

provenance.other: 'One generation passeth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ecclesiastes 1:4 is also the KJV's only verse in which one generation passes and another comes as a single proposition.
provenance.significance: Recover the rest of Ecclesiastes 1:4 and the borrowing turns against the speaker: 'One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.' The Preacher's point is that the land outlasts everyone who walks on it, which is a statement of futility. Lehi's point in this chapter is that the land is covenanted to his seed forever and will be blessed or cursed according to what the generations do on it. He has taken the Preacher's sentence about the permanence of the earth and used it to introduce bloodsheds and visitations — the same observation read as warning rather than as vanity.

1:12.note: 'As one generation passeth to another, there shall be bloodsheds and great visitations among them.' The KJV says 'One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh' once, and the Book of Mormon compresses it to a single subordinate clause. Ecclesiastes is not a book the Book of Mormon draws on often, which is part of why the singleton is worth recording; and the compression is the argument, since Ecclesiastes uses the sentence to say that nothing changes and Lehi uses it to say what will change.

1:13.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

provenance.other: 'From the dust' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:2, and 'shake thyself from the dust' is that same singleton. 'Awake, awake' occurs at Isaiah 51:9, 51:17 and 52:1 and nowhere else in the KJV. The Book of Mormon phrase 'arise from the dust' occurs in no KJV verse at all: it is a recombination of Isaiah 52:2's two imperatives, which the KJV gives in the reverse order ('Shake thyself from the dust; arise').
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:1-2 is the engine of the whole blessing, and Lehi takes all four of its imperatives and redistributes them across his speech: awake (1:13, 1:23), shake off (1:13, 1:23), arise from the dust (1:14, 1:21, 1:23), and loose the bands of the neck, which becomes the chains by which his sons are bound. What Isaiah addresses to a city — 'O captive daughter of Zion' — Lehi addresses to four sons who are about to lose a birthright, and the captivity is transposed from political to spiritual in the same breath: the chains are hell's, the dust is the grave's. The transposition is what makes the borrowing interesting, and it is complete by the second imperative. Note that this book will later transcribe Isaiah 51:24-52:2 outright at 2 Nephi 8:24-25, seven chapters after Lehi has already spoken it as his own.

1:13.note: 'O that ye would awake, awake from a deep sleep … and shake off the awful chains by which ye are bound … that they are carried away captive.' Isaiah 52:1-2 in fragments: the doubled imperative of 52:1, the shaking and the dust of 52:2, the captivity of 52:2's closing vocative, the binding of its 'bands of thy neck'. Two of the phrases are KJV singletons. Mediation is straightforwardly direct-OT here, unlike at Jacob 3:11 where the transcription at 2 Nephi 8 already stood between the source and the allusion — 2 Nephi 1 precedes that transcription, so Isaiah is the only model available to the reader at this point in the book. Note that the imperative Lehi actually coins, 'arise from the dust', is in no KJV verse; he has fused Isaiah's 'from the dust' with Isaiah's 'arise' and produced the refrain that governs verses 14, 21 and 23.

1:14.text: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;

provenance.other: 'The way of all the earth' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and both are a leader's farewell. Only 1 Kings 2:2 has it in the first person present — 'I go the way of all the earth' — which is the form 2 Nephi 1:14 reproduces word for word, eight words in sequence.
provenance.alternative: Joshua 23:14 is the other candidate and shares the theme of a land promise kept; but Joshua reads 'this day I am going the way of all the earth', and the Book of Mormon has David's tense, not Joshua's.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 2:1-4 is the KJV's model deathbed charge and 2 Nephi 1 reproduces it whole, not in one phrase but in four: David says 'I go the way of all the earth' (2:2) and Lehi says it verbatim at 1:14; David says 'be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man' and Lehi says 'arise from the dust, my sons, and be men' at 1:21; David says 'keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments' and Lehi says 'observe the statutes and the judgments of the Lord' at 1:16; David says 'that thou mayest prosper' and Lehi says 'ye shall prosper in the land' at 1:20. The catalogue has already found 1 Kings 2:3 behind 1 Nephi 2:20, where Lehi first states the covenant formula. What 2 Nephi 1 does is complete the borrowing: having taken David's promise at the start of his journey, Lehi now takes David's death. And the metalepsis is exact — 1 Kings 2 is a dying father transferring a kingdom past the sons who would have had it by right, which is precisely what verses 28-29 of this chapter do to Laman.

1:14.note: 'A few more days, and I go the way of all the earth.' Eight words of 1 Kings 2:2 in sequence, from one of the KJV's two verses that contain the phrase and the only one in this tense. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because a complete clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. The reason to read it as the whole charge rather than a tag is that three further elements of 1 Kings 2:2-4 turn up in the next seven verses of the same speech, in the source's order.

1:14.text: When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.

provenance.other: 'Shall not return' occurs in exactly thirteen KJV verses, but only Job 16:22 combines it with a few of something and with going a way: 'When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.' Job 10:21 is the same thought — 'Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness'.
provenance.alternative: The famous English form of this sentiment is not biblical at all. Hamlet's 'undiscovered country, from whose bourn no traveller returns' is closer to the Book of Mormon's wording than any KJV verse is, and 'traveller' — the 1830's spelling, modernized to 'traveler' in 1920 — is Shakespeare's word here, not the King James translators'. The catalogue records the KJV candidate and flags the non-biblical one honestly rather than suppressing it.
provenance.significance: Job 16:22 sits immediately before Job's turn to the grave and the eye that shall no more see good, and its structure is the structure of this half-verse: a short reckoning of time, then a going, then a road with no return. The Book of Mormon has the same three elements in the same order and has interleaved them with 1 Kings 2:2, so that a single sentence carries a dying king's charge and a suffering man's arithmetic at once. What Job supplies that 1 Kings does not is the finality; what 1 Kings supplies that Job does not is the command.

1:14.note: 'From whence no traveller can return: a few more days, and I go the way of all the earth.' Read against Job 16:22, 'When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return' — three elements shared (a few of a time-unit, going a way, no return) in the source's own sequence, with 'years' shortened to 'days'. Held at moderate because each element is ordinary on its own and because the nearest English parallel to the whole clause is Hamlet, not scripture; see provenance.alternative, which is a flag for Wilson rather than a settled judgment.

1:14.text: Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

provenance.other: 'And arise from the' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:14, as does 'awake thou that sleepest'. It is the KJV's only verse pairing an imperative to awake with an imperative to arise, and 'Awake! and arise from the dust' differs from it by a single word. The Book of Mormon's own phrase 'arise from the dust' occurs in exactly no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:1-2 supplies both verbs independently and is the chapter's demonstrable source (see 1:13); Ephesians may be doing nothing here that Isaiah is not already doing.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:14 is itself an unattributed scriptural citation — 'Wherefore he saith' — and what it is citing is generally taken to be Isaiah, which makes it the New Testament's own compression of the awake-and-arise material this chapter is working from. If the Book of Mormon has it, then the same fragment reaches 2 Nephi 1 twice, once through Isaiah 52 and once through Paul's condensation of it, and the tell is the word 'dead': Isaiah has dust and no death, Ephesians has death and no dust, and Lehi — speaking of the grave two clauses later — has both.

1:14.note: 'Awake! and arise from the dust.' One word away from Ephesians 5:14's 'Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead', which the machine stream caught as a four-word run. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because Isaiah 52:1-2 accounts for the same words and is independently demonstrated in the previous verse; what Ephesians adds is the imperative pairing itself, which Isaiah gives in the reverse order and across a clause boundary.
1:14.whyNot: Everything Ephesians 5:14 supplies, Isaiah 52:1-2 supplies as well, and Isaiah supplies the dust that Ephesians lacks. A reader who takes the whole refrain as Isaianic loses nothing except the neatness of the one-word substitution.

1:15.text: The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.

provenance.other: 'Everlasting arms' is a KJV singleton at Deuteronomy 33:27; the Book of Mormon's 'the arms of his love' occurs in no KJV verse, and 'in the arms of' occurs in none either.
provenance.alternative: 'Encircled about eternally in the arms of his love' may be Lehi's own figure and owe nothing to Deuteronomy; the shared element is one noun.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 33 is the KJV's one chapter that is a dying leader's blessing pronounced over sons tribe by tribe, which is the literary form of 2 Nephi 1-4 exactly: Lehi blesses Laman and Lemuel and Sam together, then Zoram, then Jacob, then Joseph, then the children of the sons. The verse that supplies the arms is the verse that closes the blessing of Israel as a whole, and its content is refuge — 'The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.' Lehi's line takes the same image and turns it from protection into embrace, and the adverb he uses, 'eternally', is Deuteronomy 33:27's 'eternal God' in adverbial form.

1:15.note: 'The Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell: I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.' The verbal contact is one noun and an adverb, so this is proposed on the genre rather than the wording: Deuteronomy 33 is the model final blessing, and this is the moment in Lehi's final blessing where he says what has become of him. 'Redeemed my soul' is itself a KJV phrase, at 2 Samuel 4:9 and 1 Kings 1:29, in both places David's oath formula — which is worth noting given that the next verse but one runs on David's deathbed charge.
1:15.whyNot: One noun. 'Arms' is not distinctive enough to establish dependence on its own, and Deuteronomy 33:27's arms are underneath as a support while Lehi's encircle as an embrace; the images are not the same image. Kept because the chapter's form is Deuteronomy 33's form and because the KJV has the phrase exactly once.

1:16.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: 'The statutes and the judgments' in that exact article-bearing form occurs in exactly no KJV verse; 'his statutes and his judgments' occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 30:16 and Psalm 147:19. What identifies 1 Kings 2:3 is not the phrase in isolation but its position two verses after 'I go the way of all the earth', which 2 Nephi 1:14 has just quoted, and which occurs in exactly two KJV verses.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 30:16 has the same triad of commandments, statutes and judgments and is the source of the Deuteronomic formula generally; Psalm 19:9's 'the judgments of the LORD' is what the machine stream proposed and is filed in the register.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has already placed 1 Kings 2:3 behind 1 Nephi 2:20, the covenant promise Lehi receives on leaving Jerusalem. Its return here closes a bracket that runs the length of Lehi's life in the text: he begins with David's charge to Solomon as a promise and ends with it as a valediction. The choice of source is not neutral, because 1 Kings 2 is a succession narrative in which the charge is followed immediately by instructions to settle scores with Joab and Shimei — and 2 Nephi 1 likewise moves from the statutes and the judgments straight to what is to be done about Laman.

1:16.note: 'Remember to observe the statutes and the judgments of the Lord: behold, this hath been the anxiety of my soul, from the beginning.' The pairing is Deuteronomic and common; what makes 1 Kings 2:3 the source here is proximity in the source rather than rarity in the phrase. Two verses earlier the Book of Mormon quoted 1 Kings 2:2 verbatim, four verses later it will restate 1 Kings 2:3's 'that thou mayest prosper', and 1 Nephi 2:20 already drew the same verse. Three contacts with one short passage inside seven verses is the argument.

1:17.text: He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.

provenance.other: 'Hardness of your hearts' — second person plural, both nouns plural — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:8. Mark 10:5 has the singular 'the hardness of your heart' and Mark 3:5 has 'the hardness of their hearts', which is the form 1 Nephi uses of Laman and Lemuel in the third person. The Book of Mormon has the pronoun and the number right for a father addressing his sons to their faces.
provenance.significance: The pronoun is the finding. Three KJV verses carry this phrase and each is grammatically distinct, and the Book of Mormon has used each of them in its correct setting: Mark 3:5's 'their' in narration about the brothers, Matthew 19:8's 'your' here, where Lehi is speaking to them. In Matthew the phrase concedes something — Moses permitted divorce because of it, so the hardness is a fact the law accommodated rather than a fault it punished. Lehi's use is the opposite: he fears that the hardness will bring the wrath rather than a concession, which is what Jesus goes on to say in the same verse ('but from the beginning it was not so').

1:17.note: 'I have feared, lest for the hardness of your hearts, lest the Lord your God should come out in the fulness of his wrath.' A KJV singleton in the exact form used. The pronoun check is the point (ADJUDICATING §4): the KJV has three hardness-of-heart phrases distinguished only by pronoun and number, and this one is Matthew's. 'The fulness of his wrath' has no KJV source — the machine's proposal of Job 20:22 is filed in the register — so the borrowed material is the diagnosis, not the sentence.

1:18.text: And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.

provenance.other: The KJV states the devil's captivity of the will once: 'the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will'. 'Taken captive by him at his will' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:26; 'snare of the devil' occurs in exactly two, 1 Timothy 3:7 and 2 Timothy 2:26, and only the second adds the taking captive and the will. 'The will of the devil' occurs in exactly no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 'Led according to the will and captivity of the Devil' is an odd English phrase — two abstract nouns coordinated where a reader expects one — and 2 Timothy 2:26 explains it: the source has both nouns, 'taken captive' and 'at his will', in one clause, and the Book of Mormon has compressed the clause into a pair. The context in 2 Timothy is instruction about how to correct those who oppose themselves, 'if God peradventure will give them repentance', which is the situation Lehi is in for the whole of this chapter: a man arguing with sons he still hopes will recover themselves. That is also where the chapter's chains come from, and it lets 1:13's captivity and 1:18's captivity be read as one figure.

1:18.note: 'Ye are visited by sword, and by famine, and are hated, and are led according to the will and captivity of the Devil.' The clause is a compression of the KJV's one statement that the devil takes men captive at his will. The first half of the verse — sword and famine — is Jeremiah's standing pair and identifies no source; the register records the machine's proposal there. What is not formulaic is the coordination of will and captivity, which exists in the KJV in a single verse.

1:20.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: 'Prosper in the land' occurs in exactly no KJV verse; 1 Kings 2:3 has 'that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest', and 'the way of all the earth', quoted six verses earlier at 1:14, occurs in exactly two KJV verses of which 1 Kings 2:2 is one. See the full argument for the source at 1 Nephi 2:20.
provenance.significance: The verse announces its own mediation — 'and he hath said' — and what was said is 1 Nephi 2:20, the promise Lehi received in the wilderness. So the proximate model is the Book of Mormon's own earlier text and the ultimate model is David's charge to Solomon, which is exactly the layering the catalogue's mediation field exists to record. The second half is the interesting half: 1 Nephi 2:21 gave the sanction as being 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', and here it hardens into first-person divine speech, 'cut off from my presence' — which is a KJV singleton, and a priestly one.

1:20.note: 'He hath said, that inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land; but inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall be cut off from my presence.' This is the Book of Mormon's covenant formula in its canonical form, and the verse presents it as a quotation of something already said. What it quotes is 1 Nephi 2:20-21, where the catalogue placed 1 Kings 2:3. Recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM for that reason rather than as a fresh contact with 1 Kings.

1:20.text: Say unto them, Whosoever he be of all your seed among your generations, that goeth unto the holy things, which the children of Israel hallow unto the LORD, having his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.

provenance.other: 'Cut off from my presence' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 22:3. The commoner biblical formula is 'cut off from among his people' or 'from the presence of the LORD' in the third person; the first-person possessive is Leviticus 22:3's alone.
provenance.alternative: 1 Nephi 2:21 already has 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', so the phrase may simply be that earlier Book of Mormon sentence recast into direct speech, with no fresh contact with Leviticus.
provenance.significance: Leviticus 22:3 is a purity statute: a priest who approaches the holy things while unclean is cut off from God's presence. It is the KJV's one use of the exact phrase, and it puts the sanction in the first person because it is God legislating about his own sanctuary. What the Book of Mormon does with it is to move the sanction from the sanctuary to a land — the uncleanness that severs a man from the presence is now disobedience on the land of promise — which is the same substitution the chapter has made twice already, at 1:7 where Eden's cursed ground becomes a cursed land and at 1:13 where Zion's captivity becomes hell's.

1:20.note: 'Ye shall be cut off from my presence.' A KJV singleton, and the shift into the first person is what identifies it: 1 Nephi 2:21 says 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', the ordinary form, and here Lehi reports God speaking, which is the form Leviticus 22:3 has. Recorded at moderate because the recasting could be the Book of Mormon's own and needs no source.

1:21.text: And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.

provenance.other: 'With sorrow to the grave' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 42:38, 44:29 and 44:31 — and all three are Jacob, or his sons quoting Jacob, about what his sons will do to him.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one formula for a father brought to the grave by grief over his sons belongs entirely to Jacob and the Joseph narrative, and it is spoken in each case about the loss of the youngest and best-loved. 2 Nephi 1 is Jacob's situation with the parts redistributed: an old man, sons who have already tried to kill the favoured brother once (1:24, 'ye sought to take away his life'), and a father who says in so many words that their conduct will decide whether he goes down in grief. Recovering the source makes the chapter's family plot legible — Lehi is speaking as Jacob, and the son he is defending will be renamed Joseph's line before the book is done.

1:21.note: 'That I might not be brought down with grief and sorrow to the grave, arise from the dust, my sons, and be men.' The KJV says 'bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave' three times and only ever of Jacob; the Book of Mormon drops the gray hairs and adds 'grief', keeping the verb and the prepositional phrase. Note what the same sentence then does: 'be men' answers 1 Kings 2:2's 'shew thyself a man', so a Jacob clause and a David clause stand in one sentence, which is what the whole chapter has been doing since verse 14.

1:22.text: And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

provenance.other: 'Both soul and body' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 10:18 and Matthew 10:28. Only Matthew makes it the object of destruction. 'A just God' is itself a KJV singleton, at Isaiah 45:21, 'a just God and a Saviour'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 10:18 has the phrase and this book transcribes that verse at 2 Nephi 20:18, so a reader might reasonably look there first.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decided by one word and it is worth stating plainly. Both KJV verses that contain 'both soul and body' were available to this book, and one of them, Isaiah 10:18, is transcribed inside 2 Nephi itself at 20:18. But in Isaiah the phrase is a simile for the consuming of a forest and carries no threat of judgment on a person; in Matthew it is the thing God is able to do in hell, and it is set against what men can do, which is kill the body only. 2 Nephi 1:22 has 'unto the destruction, yea, the eternal destruction of both soul and body' — destruction, eternity, and both nouns as its object. That is Matthew's sentence and not Isaiah's, in a book that demonstrably had Isaiah's in front of it. tools/mediation-check.py declines the case because the two verses do not diverge at a point the Book of Mormon reproduces verbatim; the decision is made on which verse's predicate survives.

1:22.note: 'That ye may not incur the displeasure of a just God upon you, unto the destruction, yea, the eternal destruction of both soul and body.' Two KJV verses have the phrase and this one takes the New Testament's, on the evidence of the predicate: Matthew's God is 'able to destroy both soul and body in hell', Isaiah's fire merely consumes a forest 'both soul and body' as a figure. 'A just God' in the same sentence is a second KJV singleton, from Isaiah 45:21, where the point is that a just God is also a Saviour — the half Lehi does not quote.

1:23.text: The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.

provenance.other: 'Awake out of sleep' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:11, and 'put on the armour' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:12 — consecutive verses, and the only place in the KJV where the two imperatives stand in that order. 'Works of darkness', the middle term Lehi replaces with chains, occurs in exactly two.
provenance.significance: The sequence is the finding. Romans 13:11-12 runs awake out of sleep, then cast off the works of darkness, then put on the armour; 2 Nephi 1 runs awake from a deep sleep (1:13), then shake off the chains (1:13 and again here), then put on the armour (1:23). Three steps, same order, ten verses apart, and each of the two outer steps is a KJV singleton in Romans. Paul's reason for the sequence is eschatological — the night is far spent — and Lehi's is that he is dying, which is the same argument scaled to one man. What the Book of Mormon substitutes is the middle term: Paul casts off works, Lehi shakes off chains, and the chains are Isaiah 52:2's bands, which is how the Isaiah refrain and the Romans sequence end up sharing a single sentence.

1:23.note: 'Awake, my sons; put on the armor of righteousness. Shake off the chains with which ye are bound, and come forth out of obscurity, and arise from the dust.' Two KJV singletons from consecutive verses of Romans 13, deployed in Romans' own order across this chapter. Note the 1830 spelling 'armor', which is American and not the KJV's 'armour' — the first edition here modernizes rather than preserving the source's orthography, which is the reverse of the usual case (CONVENTIONS §8) and means the borrowing is slightly less visible in every edition of the Book of Mormon than it is in the King James Bible.

1:23.text: By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,

provenance.other: 'Armour of righteousness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Romans 13:12 has 'the armour of light' and Ephesians 6:11 'the whole armour of God'; neither is the phrase used here.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has taken the imperative from Romans 13:12 and the genitive from 2 Corinthians 6:7, which are the KJV's two armour verses outside Ephesians, and fused them into a phrase that is in neither. What 2 Corinthians 6:7 supplies with the word is its setting: Paul is listing the credentials by which he commends himself as a minister — 'by the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness' — and three verses of this chapter later Lehi will defend Nephi's ministry in the same terms, 'the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him' (1:26). Two of Paul's three phrases, from the same clause, turn up in Lehi's defence of his son.

1:23.note: 'Put on the armor of righteousness.' A KJV singleton supplies the noun phrase and Romans 13:12 supplies the verb; the composite is recorded as two rows because each half is separately a singleton and each carries its own context. The reason to keep 2 Corinthians 6:7 rather than fold it into the Romans row is 1:26, where the word of truth and the power of God from the same verse of 2 Corinthians reappear together.

1:23.text: And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness.

provenance.other: 'Obscurity' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and all three are Isaiah: 29:18, 58:10, 59:9. Only 29:18 has anything coming out of obscurity.
provenance.alternative: 'Come forth out of obscurity' may be Lehi's own phrase; the word is rare in the KJV but not distinctive of any one of its three verses beyond the preposition.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:18 is the verse in which the deaf hear the words of the book and the blind see out of obscurity, and 2 Nephi 27 will expand that whole chapter into the book's central prophecy about its own coming forth — the sealed book, the words of the book delivered to one who is not learned. 2 Nephi 27:29 renders 29:18 directly. So when Lehi tells his sons to come forth out of obscurity, he is using, twenty-six chapters early, a word that the book will later claim for the emergence of the book itself.

1:23.note: 'Come forth out of obscurity, and arise from the dust.' The KJV uses 'obscurity' three times, all in Isaiah, and only 29:18 has sight coming out of it. Recorded as an echo because a single rare word in a different construction is all the contact there is; kept because of where the word goes later in this same book. The clause it stands in is Isaiah 52:2's, so the verse fuses two Isaiah passages the book will transcribe at 2 Nephi 8 and 2 Nephi 27 respectively.

1:24.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: 'Perish with hunger' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:17. The KJV's other famine language is 'die by famine', 'consumed by the famine', 'famished'.
provenance.alternative: Starving in a wilderness needs no source, and the phrase is short.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one 'perish with hunger' is the sentence in which the prodigal son comes to himself, and everything about its transposition is an inversion. In Luke the words are spoken by the younger son who took his portion and wasted it and who now returns to a father who will restore him over the elder brother's protest. Here they are spoken by the father, about the elder brothers, and what saves them from perishing is the younger son — the one whose birthright the elder brothers are about to lose to him four verses later. Luke's parable is the KJV's one story about which son gets the father's blessing at the end, which is the question 2 Nephi 1:28-29 exists to settle.

1:24.note: 'Were it not for him, we must have perished with hunger in the wilderness.' A three-word KJV singleton, and the case rests entirely on its rarity plus where it comes from. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and the situation is one a writer could describe in those words without a source; the reason for keeping it is that the chapter's business in the next five verses is a contested inheritance between an elder son and a younger, which is the parable's business too.

1:26.text: Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.

provenance.other: 'Sharpness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction' (2 Corinthians 13:10). The Book of Mormon has the noun, the verb 'used', and the word 'power' in the same relation to it.
provenance.significance: The whole of Lehi's defence of Nephi is 2 Corinthians 13 in narrative. Paul's closing chapter is a defence of his own severity to a congregation that has accused him of being bold only at a distance: he writes sharply, he says, so that he need not use sharpness in person, and the sharpness is authorized by 'the power which the Lord hath given me'. Lehi's sons accuse Nephi of sharpness and of seeking power and authority; Lehi answers that the sharpness was 'the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him', which is Paul's defence with Paul's two nouns. And the verse after Paul's is 'Finally, brethren, farewell … be of one mind', which 2 Nephi 1:21 has already used — 'be determined in one mind' — five verses earlier. Two consecutive verses of Paul's own valediction supply two clauses of Lehi's.

1:26.note: 'Ye say that he hath used sharpness … but behold, his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God, which was in him.' The KJV uses the word 'sharpness' once, and in that one place it is coupled to power and to a minister's authority to be severe — which is precisely the coupling the Book of Mormon makes and precisely the accusation Lehi is rebutting. This is as close to a certain link as an unquoted three-word contact gets; it is held at high rather than certain only because the noun is a natural English word for the thing being described. Note also that 2 Corinthians 6:7's 'word of truth … power of God … armour of righteousness' stands behind 1:23 and the phrase 'the power of the word of God' here.

1:27.text: And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel,

provenance.other: 'Open my mouth boldly' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:19; 'utterance' occurs in exactly five KJV verses, of which Ephesians 6:19 is the one that pairs it with an opened mouth. 'No man can shut it' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 3:8.
provenance.alternative: 'Opened his mouth' is common KJV narration, and 'utterance' could come from Acts 2:4, where the Spirit gives it — which is arguably closer to the theology of this verse than Ephesians is.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 6 supplies both ends of Lehi's defence of Nephi and it does so from the two halves of one paragraph. The armour of verse 23 is Ephesians 6:11-17's figure, even though the exact genitive came from 2 Corinthians 6:7; and the utterance of verse 27 is Ephesians 6:19-20, the request that closes the armour passage — 'that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly … that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.' Lehi's word for what his sons resented, at 1:26, is 'manifesting boldly'. So the chapter has put on Paul's armour and then asked for Paul's boldness of speech, in the source's own order, and has attributed both to the Spirit rather than to the man — which is the point Lehi needs to make to sons who have accused Nephi of seeking power for himself.

1:27.note: 'It was the spirit of the Lord which was in him, which opened his mouth to utterance, that he could not shut it.' Read against Ephesians 6:19: an opened mouth, an utterance given rather than possessed, and boldness — which is the word this speech uses one verse earlier. The closing clause is a second rare phrase, Revelation 3:8's 'no man can shut it', turned from a door into a mouth. Held at moderate because 'utterance' has five KJV homes and Acts 2:4's is a live alternative; the reason for preferring Ephesians is 1:23, where the same paragraph of Ephesians has already been in view.

1:29.text: And he said, Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing. And he said, Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?

provenance.other: 'Taken away my blessing' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 27:36 — Esau's protest that Jacob 'took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing'. Genesis 49:3-4 is the other transfer, Reuben the firstborn told 'thou shalt not excel'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's family plot stated in its source's words, and the assignment of the words is the finding. In Genesis 27:36 it is the wronged elder brother who says a blessing has been taken away; in 2 Nephi 1:29 it is the father who says it, and he says it in advance, as a condition. That single change converts a theft into a judicial act — what Rebekah and Jacob accomplish by deceit at Isaac's bedside, Lehi announces openly from his own. The book has used Genesis 27 before, at 1 Nephi 4:21, where Nephi obtains the plates by wearing another man's clothes and answering to his name; a reader who holds both passages together sees the younger brother acquire the record by Jacob's method and then receive the blessing by Jacob's inheritance, with the father's consent supplied the second time.

1:29.note: 'If ye will not hearken unto him, I take away my first blessing, yea, even my blessing, and it shall rest upon him.' The KJV states the taking away of a blessing once, in Esau's mouth. Lehi transposes it into the first person of the man who gives the blessing and adds the birthright's technical term — 'my first blessing' — which pairs with Genesis 27:36's other clause, 'he took away my birthright'. Both halves of Esau's complaint are therefore present, redistributed. Genesis 49:3-4, Jacob demoting Reuben on his own deathbed, is the composite that supplies the setting.
